title: The Emerald Tablet — the whole text, line by line
desc: A dozen lines that ruled alchemy for a thousand years: the Arabic origin, the Latin vulgate, what each verse claims, Newton's translation, and why there is no emerald and no Egypt.
tldr: Step 06 took one sentence apart. Now take the whole text: twelve or so lines, first attested in Arabic in the eighth or ninth century, translated into Latin in the twelfth, copied by every serious alchemist in Europe including Newton, and never once found on an actual tablet. Read straight through, it is not mysterious at all — it is a compressed operating procedure with a cosmological warrant at the front.
body:
The Tablet is short enough to read in ninety seconds and dense enough that people have argued about it for eight hundred years. Below is the text, in our working translation from the medieval Latin vulgate, with what each part is doing. The manuscript tradition varies on wording; where variants matter, we say so.

The frame: the claim of authority

“True, without falsehood, certain and most true.” The text opens by insisting on its own reliability — a standard move in technical literature of the period, and a signal that what follows is meant as instruction rather than speculation. It closes the same way, with the speaker naming himself Hermes Trismegistus, “having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world”. Frame at the front, signature at the back, procedure in between.

The warrant: why any of this should work

“That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing.” This is step 06's sentence, and in context its job is obvious: it is the premise that licenses everything after it. Then: “And as all things were from one, by the mediation of one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation.” A single source, a single mediating principle, and — the operative word — adaptation. Things become other things by being adapted, not by magic.

The parentage: sun, moon, wind, earth

“Its father is the sun, its mother the moon; the wind carried it in its belly, the earth is its nurse.” Alchemical readers took these as material designations — sun for gold or sulphur, moon for silver or mercury, wind for a volatile phase, earth for the residue — and the tradition of decoding them is itself centuries old. Nothing in the text says which reading is right. That ambiguity is not a flaw; it is how a recipe stays usable across different laboratory practices.

The procedure: separate, ascend, descend, receive

“Separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently, with great skill.” Then: “It ascends from earth to heaven and descends again to earth, and receives the power of the higher and the lower things.” This is the core, and it is a loop, not a ladder. Something is refined, raised, returned, and comes back carrying what it gained. In laboratory terms this reads as distillation and reflux — vapour rising, condensing, falling back, repeated until the substance changes character. In the reading that later mystics preferred, it describes a person.

Note the two adverbs in the separation line: gently and with great skill. Whatever else the Tablet is, it is not a text that recommends force.

The result and the claim

“Thus you will have the glory of the whole world, and all obscurity will flee from you.” The promise is knowledge and mastery, stated in the register of its period. Then the last technical line: “This is the strong power of every power, for it will conquer every subtle thing and penetrate every solid.” The thing being made is described as universally effective — which is why later readers identified it with the philosophers' stone, though the Tablet never uses that phrase.

Where it comes from, and where it does not

The earliest surviving version sits inside the Arabic Kitab sirr al-khaliqa, attributed to Balinas, dated by most scholars to the eighth or ninth century. Latin translations follow in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and from then on the text is everywhere: in alchemical compendia, in printed collections, in manuscripts owned by mathematicians. Isaac Newton made his own English translation, preserved in Keynes MS 28 at King's College, Cambridge — a reminder that the line between alchemy and early modern science is not where popular history puts it.

What we do not have: a Greek original, an Egyptian original, any physical tablet, or any citation of the text before the Arabic material. The discovery legends — found in a tomb, clutched in the hands of Hermes, written on green stone — belong to the reception layer. They are worth knowing as stories about how authority was manufactured, not as history.

Frame · warrant · parentage · procedure · result. Read in that order the Tablet stops being an oracle and becomes what it is: a compact set of instructions with its justification stated first.
facts: About twelve lines, depending on the version
Arabic, in the Kitab sirr al-khaliqa, 8th–9th c.

None; no emerald, no tomb, no archaeological trace
faq: Is the Tablet alchemy or philosophy?

Both, and the split is ours rather than theirs. It gives a cosmological premise and then a procedure, which is exactly how technical literature of the period argued. Forcing it to be only spiritual or only chemical is a modern habit.

For study, read a modern scholarly rendering with the Latin alongside; the wording varies between manuscripts, and any translation that hides that is selling certainty it does not have. Newton's version is worth reading as a historical document, not as an authority.
Why did such a short text matter so much?

Because it is portable and it authorises. A dozen memorable lines that explain why an operation should work are more useful to a practitioner than a treatise — and easier to copy into the front of a notebook, which is precisely what people did for centuries.

Kevin van Bladel, The Arabic Hermes (Oxford UP, 2009) — the transmission context.
